newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Negotiated Zaire transition on track, says envoy.
newsitem.headline: Negotiated Zaire transition on track, says envoy.

text.p: U.S. and South African mediators in Zaire's civil war said after a meeting in Cape Town on Tuesday that diplomatic efforts to avoid a bloody showdown in Kinshasa were still on track.
"I had a very good meeting with Deputy President Thabo Mbeki...we're working very closely," U.S. envoy Bill Richardson told reporters after the hour-long meeting.
"The South Africans are taking the lead...I would think the next thing is up to the South African government, they're doing a lot of work, a lot of good diplomacy.
"The peace process is very much on track, I'm very encouraged," Richardson said, adding that he would travel on to Paris on Wednesday to brief the French government.

Frank Chikane, a senior aide to Mbeki, said South Africa still hoped Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko would hold another round of talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila in the coming week, as agreed.
Asked about reports that Kabila's men could reach the capital Kinshasa within days, Chikane said:

"I believe we need to be positive. We want to find a solution because we wouldn't want to see a bloodbath, we don't want to see many innocent people die. We want to make sure there's a peaceful transition to a form of authority that's going to take over responsibility."

But South African analysts, noting reports that Mobutu was now scheduled to leave the country on Wednesday for two days in Gabon, said it seemed only a matter of days before the rebel army would complete its takeover of the vast central African state by force.
"I think this is the first stage of Mr Mobutu stepping down," said Greg Mills, national director of South Africa's Institute of International Affairs.

"He could use this as a way to hand over power to a transitional authority as a way for him to retain some of his dignity and to hand over in a fairly orderly fashion and prevent any violence in Kinshasa," Mills told South African state radio. "I would say it's a first step in that regard. It's a face saving measure for him."
Chikane said South Africa was working on the assumption that Kabila was sticking to an assurance issued at the weekend that his troops had halted their advance several days ago.
"We're working on the basis of the statement they agreed upon. He has made that commitment himself, and that's the basis on which we work," Chikane said.
Zaire rebel radio, however, was reporting a steady advance on Kinshasa and calling on the government army to surrender.
